Sixth-generation (6G) communication systems are expected to support immersive, intent-driven, and latency-critical services through tight integration of multimodal intelligence, edge computing, and autonomous network control. In this setting, agentic AI systems can reason over heterogeneous inputs, use tools and network functions, coordinate across distributed entities, and adapt to dynamic environments. These capabilities make agentic multimodal intelligence promising for 6G applications such as semantic communications, digital twins, and zero-touch network management, but they also introduce security and privacy risks that extend beyond conventional AI and network security models. Vulnerabilities can propagate across multimodal data pipelines, memory, tools, communication interfaces, and inter-agent coordination loops. We survey multimodal intelligence and agentic AI for 6G cross-layered communication systems from the perspectives of privacy and security. We present a 6G-oriented system view spanning perception, memory, tool use, and multi-agent orchestration; analyze threat models and attack surfaces across sensing, cognition, action, memory, and communication layers; organize existing attacks into a structured taxonomy; and review mitigation strategies including prompt and memory defenses, inter-agent trust mechanisms, secure orchestration, and privacy-preserving learning. We conclude by outlining open research directions for trustworthy multimodal multi-agent 6G systems.

Furthermore, a confidence-calibrated reweighting loss is designed to integrate feature-space similarity, effectively mitigating unreliable pseudolabels and class imbalance during continuous signal acquisition. To ensure system stability and prevent the catastrophic forgetting of established neural patterns, a lightweight memory module is incorporated to regularize parameter updates within a tight latency budget. Evaluated on the BCI IV IIb and OpenBMI datasets, MOPC achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming prior methods by 2.22~\% and 3.67~\%, respectively, while keeping the per-trial adaptation latency to approximately 40--60 ms. Furthermore, the method detects subtle sub-decibel temporal variations in coupling conditions over seasonal timescales, demonstrating its capability for continuous fiber health monitoring. These results establish semblance distance analysis as a physically interpretable tool for DAS channel selection with direct applications in seismic imaging, structural health monitoring, and noise mitigation in high sensitivity systems such as gravitational wave detectors.

The fitted model reproduces the median errors of the 2.5 MHz and 5 MHz flights but underestimates the heaviest error tails. Finally, rejecting outlier fixes lowers the error far more than Kalman or particle filtering, because the remaining error is dominated by bias.

In this paper, we propose the wave processing unit (WPU), a programmable planar Mach--Zehnder interferometer (MZI) network that accelerates matrix--vector multiplications in MIMO communications. To handle arbitrary complex-valued operators, we further extend the method through singular value decomposition (SVD) and a hardware-efficient semi-unitary synthesis, avoiding redundant hardware and reducing the compilation complexity. We then apply the WPU to multiuser downlink precoding by an efficient WPU synthesis method, and compare the proposed architecture with hybrid and wave-domain ones. Numerical results demonstrate machine-precision synthesis with negligible residuals for up to $64\times64$ operators, with approximately $380\times$ faster configuration than iterative wave computing baselines. For 64-antenna, 8-user downlink precoding, WPU requires 87.5% fewer RF chains than the fully digital architecture while achieving the same sum rate under ideal hardware. These results highlight the potential of the WPU for precise, hardware-efficient wave-domain processing with rapid configuration.
comment: Submitted to IEEE journals for possible publication
☆ Training-Efficient Channel Estimation for the Multiuser Uplink Relying on Generalized Flexible Intelligent Metasurfaces
Daniel C. Araújo, André L. F. de Almeida, Lajos Hanzo
We consider uplink multiuser channel estimation for a generalized flexible intelligent metasurface at the base station, under narrowband far-field propagation and a twin-time-scale mechanical protocol: on the slow time-scale the panel translates rigidly over a planar grid, while on the fast time-scale the surface morphs along its normal direction. From orthogonal multiuser pilots, we show that each user's channel admits a fourth-order canonical polyadic tensor structure. We develop two complementary estimators: alternating least squares factorization followed by paired rotational-invariance wavevector extraction, and a tensor spatial-smoothing multiple signal classification estimator that preserves the multilinear array manifold. Both share a minimum description length front-end for automatic tensor-rank detection. We derive Kruskal identifiability conditions that relate the numbers of elements, morphing states and grid positions to the maximum number of recoverable multipath components, and show that the tensor model reconstructs the channel at panel configurations beyond the training grid. This prediction capability drives a configuration-selective multiuser transmit precoder that searches the entire motion grid without additional pilot overhead. Numerical results confirm the identifiability limits and show that, once the model order is resolved, the configuration search makes the same choice from estimated as from perfect channel state information. The reconfiguration gain over a fixed panel of identical aperture and training budget grows with the user load, and fast morphing proves valuable for conditioning the tensor factorization rather than as a source of beamforming gain.
☆ Recursive Code Evolution for Task-Oriented Semantic Communications
Yan Gong, Zheng Chu, Wei Koong Chai, Hari Mohan Pandey, Jingrui Hou, Miao Zhang, Yuanjian Li, Pei Xiao
Semantic communication jointly optimizes inference accuracy, channel use, and computation, yet the underlying communication program is typically specified before training. This paper presents ComRSI (Communications-Oriented Recursive Self-Improvement), a framework for recursively evolving that program through large-language-model-assisted code edits. A fixed agent modifies the encoder, channel adapters, decoder, loss, and training policy; a protected evaluator screens candidates under prescribed budgets and resource constraints. Accepted code and textual feedback inform subsequent proposals, while candidate weights are trained from scratch. In the original ten-generation CIFAR-100 lineage, eight accepted revisions produce an attention-pooled code achieving 74.3% test accuracy over an Additive White Gaussian Noise (AWGN) channel at 32 complex symbols per image, compared with 67.2% at 256 symbols for the initial design. The program also improves fading-channel accuracy and transfers to Tiny-ImageNet after retraining. A repeat study with ten searches per method compares ComRSI against non-recursive agents with and without textual history. Mean final search scores balancing accuracy, transmission rate, and computational cost are 0.7587, 0.7376, and 0.7089, respectively; the mean numbers of accepted revisions per search are 6.0, 5.0, and 2.1. The advantage over the memoryless agent is supported by a two-sided rank test, whereas the difference from the history-equipped agent remains statistically inconclusive at this sample size. Archived proposals show that pooling can yield a large improvement, while retained history supports subsequent refinement. These results support recursive program optimization within the evaluated setting and expose its remaining rate-robustness and compute-placement trade-offs.
☆ Cross-Area Transfer Learning for VLC-based Indoor Localization with a Transfer Efficiency Score
Masood Jan, Wafa Njima, Xun Zhang, Alexander Artemenko
Indoor localization systems are critical for Industry-4.0 applications. Visible Light Communication (VLC)-based systems offer advantages such as immunity to electromagnetic interference, high accuracy, and energy efficiency, but their performance is hindered by environmental variability across deployment areas. This paper presents a transfer learning (TL) framework for VLC-based indoor localization that enhances cross-area robustness while reducing data requirements. Using real-world measurements from four distinct areas of a Bosch manufacturing facility, we show that fine-tuning a deep neural network (DNN) pre-trained on source area data with only 40% of target-area measurements recovers 97% of full-data performance, thereby reducing the amount of target data needed. We further introduce the Transfer Efficiency Score (TES), a composite metric that identifies the most effective source models for transfer without exhaustive evaluation. Guided by TES, the framework selects the best source model, yielding localization errors as low as 40.9 cm with success rates above 86%. Validation on an unseen area confirms its generalization capability, with a 3.28 cm mean error achieved using the TES-selected source model. Overall, the proposed framework provides a scalable and data-efficient pathway for industrial VLC localization, substantially reducing deployment costs and computational burden while maintaining high accuracy in diverse and dynamic environments.
☆ Passive RF Sensing for People Counting with Dense IoT Networks
Federica Fieramosca, Vittorio Rampa, Michele D'Amico
Radio Frequency (RF) convergence, the joint use of radio signals for both communication and sensing, is gaining increasing attention in research and industry, mostly for its potential in Internet of Things (IoT) applications. By using RF signals of opportunity, such as those generate by the wireless networks, RF sensing exploits the effects of human bodies on the electromagnetic waves to detect both people presence and their movements without requiring wearable devices. In this paper, we address the problem of estimating the number of people in a monitored area covered by several RF nodes of a wireless network: to this aim, we propose a composite diffraction-based model, namely C-MAM, to capture the cumulative RF attenuation induced by multiple human bodies. Building on this model, we derive the analytical resolvability bounds that quantify the maximum number of distinguishable individuals based on the layout geometry and other physical characteristics of the wireless network. These bounds allow for the pre-deployment assessment of RF sensing performance under different scenarios.
☆ A Transfer Learning-Driven Methodology for Efficient and Sustainable Indoor Localization Using VLC
Masood Jan, Wafa Njima, Xun Zhang, Alexander Artemenko
The rapid expansion of the Internet of Things enables seamless collaboration among connected devices, making indoor localization a critical component of industrial automation. However, conventional localization techniques struggle in dynamic environments. These methods depend on extensive, frequent data collection and environment-specific calibration, limiting scalability, interoperability, and effective use of prior research while imposing significant energy penalties that hinder practical deployment. To address these challenges, we propose an energy-efficient transfer learning (TL) based approach for visible light communication based indoor localization. Our method leverages TL to tackle environmental variability, including lighting fluctuations and physical obstacles that typically degrade localization performance, while simultaneously reducing computational overhead and energy consumption compared to conventional approaches. We also introduce a novel model efficiency (ME) metric, designed to integrate localization accuracy, energy efficiency, data efficiency, and transfer gain into a single evaluative measure for comprehensive optimization. Evaluations on a real-world dataset collected from a BOSCH factory demonstrate that our model achieves a 47% improvement in localization accuracy compared to a conventional model that does not utilize TL, and achieves up to 67.5% ME with TL models, compared to only 10.4% in conventional models under high-noise conditions. These results underscore the potential of our approach to deliver a highly efficient and scalable indoor localization system suitable for energy-constrained industrial applications.
☆ Digital Particle Communication under Flow: Frequency Analysis and Pulse Design
Fatih Merdan, Ozgur B. Akan
In particle communication, particles released for different symbols can reach the receiver at overlapping times, making reliable detection difficult. This paper develops a digital communication framework that connects particle transport, pulse shaping, and receiver processing for three-dimensional free-space diffusion-advection channels. We derive the continuous-time and discrete-time frequency responses and explain how flow speed affects channel delay and bandwidth. Under advection-dominated conditions, the group delay approaches $R/V$, and the one-sided $3$-dB bandwidth scales as $V^{3/2}$. We design nonnegative, unit-energy transmit pulses using a packet-level SINR criterion that includes interference from both preceding and subsequent symbols under additive white Gaussian receiver noise. Simulations validate the analytical approximations and show that optimized pulses spread across more of the symbol interval when noise is substantial and become narrower as noise decreases. BER evaluations across SNR and symbol duration compare optimized, rectangular, and single-impulse pulses with several detection methods, identifying the operating conditions in which transmit-pulse design improves reliability.
☆ Large-size multivariate scale-free texture generation from small-size learning sets with self-attention Wasserstein-GAN ICASSP 2026
Jhonatan Ancco Cerda, Kinan Abbas, Stéphane G. Roux, Patrice Abry
Multivariate scale-free texture images are nowadays central in numerous modern applications very different in nature. A common challenging issue consists of being able to generate such multivariate textures at any arbitrary size, from a learning set of (possibly much) smaller size. Parametric models often turn out to be too restrictive for the generation of realistic textures, thus prompting neural network training-based generation. While several neural network approaches propose generation at sizes larger than training, they do not explicitly assess the quality of the generation by quantifying how well multiscale or scale-free statistics in textures are reproduced and rather rely on perceptual assessment. The present work combines convolutional Wasserstein-GAN architectures with self-attention layers to generate textures of arbitrary size while focusing on reproducing multiscale statistics, without coding a model into the loss function. The relevance of using a self-attention layer is studied. Quantitative assessment conducted on multifractal textures, representative of a broad class of multiscale textures, over ten independent trainings shows that the proposed architecture is able to generate textures with accurate statistics for sizes $8 \times 8$ larger than the originals. The results show that placing self-attention in the critic provides the most consistent performance across output sizes.

☆ Deep Reinforcement Learning Assistance for Resilient Haptic Teleoperation over a 5G Network
Georgios Kokkinis, Aitor Hernandez Herranz, Qi Zhang
Haptic teleoperation requires low-latency and reliable communication to preserve stable and responsive interaction between a human operator and a remote environment. However, network congestion can strongly degrade teleoperation performance, particularly when haptic traffic competes with other data flows for limited radio resources. This work investigates a deep reinforcement learning (DRL)-assisted teleoperation framework over an Ericsson 5G standalone (SA) testbed under different congestion and quality-of-service (QoS) configurations. In the evaluated task, a human operator uses a haptic device to steer a spaceship through a remote virtual game. The DRL agent runs inside the remote environment, hosted at the network edge, and assists the operator by blending its own actions with the operator's commands received over the 5G network. This placement gives the agent direct access to the current state of the environment, unaffected by network delay. Experimental results show that DRL assistance improves task performance under all network conditions, with the largest benefit under congestion, where it reduces mean task completion time by 20.6%. Under congestion, assisted operation even outperforms unassisted operation with QoS prioritisation, which restores latency close to the uncongested baseline.

☆ Point Cloud Transmission With Patch-Based Rate Adaptation
Shipeng Liu, Garima Bazard, Khac-Hoang Ngo, Per-Erik Forssén
We propose a joint source-channel coding (JSCC) framework for efficient wireless point cloud transmission. In the proposed scheme, the point cloud is first divided into local patches and transformed into compact latent representations, which are then mapped to symbols for transmission over a noisy channel. Our model incorporates an entropy model that exploits inter-patch spatial dependencies to estimate patch-level coding costs and allocate different numbers of symbols accordingly. Unlike existing patch-based point cloud JSCC methods that use the same transmission rate between patches, we adapt the channel usage of each patch latent representation. To exploit inter-patch dependencies without patch-by-patch autoregressive processing, we select a group of anchor patches whose features provide contextual information for entropy estimation of non-anchor ones. The framework is trained using a reconstruction loss and an entropy-based rate surrogate. Experiments on ModelNet40 demonstrate overall rate-distortion improvements over existing baselines across channel conditions.
☆ Approximate Matrix Multiplication through Joint Leverage Score Sampling
Neophytos Charalambides, Mert Pilanci, Alfred O. Hero
In this paper, we investigate approximate matrix multiplication through random sampling. Specifically, we propose using a non-uniform sampling distribution constructed from the leverage scores of the two matrices, and characterize the associated approximation error in terms of the matrix spectral norm; which is well-known to better characterize the downstream error when the matrix product operator is applied to an input vector. We provide the probability error bounds for the proposed algorithm are also given, and discuss connections to data-oblivious approximate matrix multiplication, and graph sparsification algorithms.
☆ Over-the-Air Computation with Power Amplifier Nonlinearity
David Nordlund, Ayça Özçelikkale, Zheng Chen
Over-the-air computation (AirComp) enables efficient wireless data aggregation by exploiting the superposition of signals transmitted by multiple source nodes, but its performance is sensitive to hardware impairments such as power amplifier (PA) nonlinearity. In this paper, we develop an analytical framework for coherent AirComp with PA nonlinearities and derive a closed-form expression for the receiver mean-squared error (MSE) under a memoryless polynomial PA model. Our numerical results show that power control optimized under the conventional linear-PA assumption can exhibit rapidly increasing MSE as the transmit power budget increases, whereas incorporating PA nonlinearity into the power control design prevents this degradation and maintains low MSE over the considered power range.

☆ Data-Driven Localization of Magneto-Mechanical Resonators from Time Signals
Artyom Tsanda, Konrad Scheffler, Sarah Reiss, Jonas Faltinath, Janik Bach, Florian Thieben, Pascal Stagge, Fabian Mohn, Tobias Knopp
Magneto-mechanical resonators (MMRs) are a recently introduced sensor technology for tracking and sensing applications that enables effective miniaturization down to the millimeter regime. However, estimating sensor parameters such as position from raw signals remains computationally challenging, because it requires solving a nonlinear inverse problem with computationally demanding objective function evaluations. In this work, we show how a deep learning method can accelerate this process by directly learning the inverse mapping from the measured signals. We consider the localization problem as an example and show that a convolutional-transformer regressor trained on simulated data with recorded noise can generalize to experimental data. The method achieves a median Euclidean distance error of 7 mm, which is comparable to the size of the sensor and corresponds to 6% of the size of a single coil. These results suggest that deep learning is a promising approach for rapid estimation of MMR parameters.
☆ Control-Field and Quasi-Cyclic Code Recovery in Starlink Downlink Signals
Haoyan Liu, Yichuan Ma, Min Yang, Chengguang Li
Public descriptions of the Starlink downlink specify synchronization sequences, edge pilots, and predictable symbol templates, but leave the coded control fields and explicit payload-code representations largely unresolved. We examine one continuous complex-baseband capture spanning approximately 24 ms and recover control and coding structure beyond those predictable elements. Reference-phase removal exposes terminated rate-1/3 convolutional control blocks with constraint length seven and a group-level cyclic redundancy check. A conditional descriptor layout predicts sequential allocations through per-codeword symbol rounding, agreeing exactly with independently estimated endpoints in 16 of 18 frame records and within two symbols in the remaining records. Quasi-cyclic closure, binary elimination, and sparse dual checks yield explicit systematic code representations at rates 1/2 and 5/8. Frozen encoders predict 78,848, 9,984, and 811,008 reserved parity bits for three formats without disagreement. A rank-deficient long-code fit is completed within a declared finite structural family, and shared encoders are tested across modulation formats. The recovered representations explain observed coded symbols; they do not authenticate transmitter-standard identities or plaintext semantics. Two high-order formats have only one target field each, while codes 28 and 37 admit verified shortened cores with unexplained extra bits and code 4 remains unresolved.
☆ Beyond Task Relevance: Interaction-Aware Semantic Communication for Wireless Agent Collaboration
Yiru Wang, Pengxin Guan, Xiumei Deng, Zehui Xiong
Semantic communication in multi-agent systems often assumes that task-relevant information benefits the team once delivered. Yet semantic sharing can alter the receiver's decision and increase inter-agent dependence, potentially reducing team utility. Motivated by this phenomenon, we develop an interaction-aware framework for wireless collaboration between heterogeneous agents. We analytically relate communication-induced dependence to expected best-of-team utility and define a team-level semantic value for candidate messages. We consider semantic units at different abstraction levels and formulate a deadline- and power-constrained problem that maximizes predicted team-level net surplus. We derive an interaction-aware policy that selects at most one unit and its transmit power, or chooses not to transmit. Experiments on two verifier-scored optimization tasks show that full-solution exchange induces stronger structural convergence and more adverse team-level effects, whereas method hints exhibit pronounced directionality. Across the evaluated power budgets, our policy achieves the highest net team-level surplus while consuming less energy than semantic-aware and full-solution baselines.
☆ Precision-Aware Hierarchical Spectrum Search for Finite-Precision MUSIC DOA Estimation
Linyun Yue, Chuang Yang, Jierui Chen, Mugen Peng
Dense-grid spectrum search is computationally costly for multiple signal classification (MUSIC) direction-of-arrival (DOA) estimation, and low-precision evaluation can introduce numerical errors that distort candidate selection. This paper proposes precision-aware hierarchical MUSIC (PAH-MUSIC), a multistage framework that coordinates arithmetic precision, angular grids, and candidate windows in spectrum evaluation, while covariance estimation and eigendecomposition remain in FP64. Stage-dependent precision is assigned from coarse candidate discovery to final DOA estimation. Under bounded perturbations and local spectral growth, a conditional displacement bound gives a sufficient window-width condition for retained, correctly associated candidates. For a two-stage continuous cost model with fixed precision weights and window coefficients, a closed-form optimal coarse step and a cost-gain condition are derived. Simulations with two separated sources and 500 frames at each tested signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) from -10 to 15 dB show that FP8, FP16, and FP32 coarse searches followed by FP64 refinement achieve DOA root-mean-square errors close to a baseline using FP64 at both search stages. Relative to that baseline, the selected configurations reduce weighted spectrum-evaluation cost by 28.36\%--44.66\% under the adopted precision weights.

☆ The Metrology Atlas: describing recorded physiological data as a measurement system, with VitalDB as a first application
Andrew J. Goodwin
Every value in a recorded physiological dataset is a pair: a recorded time and a recorded value. Neither is the truth. The time comes from a clock that drifts and is corrected in jumps, and often describes a window that ended earlier. The value was quantised, rounded, sometimes heaped by hand, and measured by an instrument with its own error. We present the Metrology Atlas, a dataset-independent way of describing a recorded dataset as a measurement system, and its first application, to VitalDB, an open dataset of 6,388 surgical patients, as a proof of principle. For every variable, the atlas states what was measured, the measurement model linking it to the recorded pair, and what is known about the true time and true value given a record. Each part of the model carries its evidence: 69 studies, 49 parameters and 54 observations, each marked as measured, derived, estimated or assumed. The atlas maps 11 clocks and 14 devices into one timing network, and closes loops in that network to test its own model. Synchronisation reduces the median timing error between the EEG and ECG from 794 ms to 42 ms, and between ventilator and monitor waveforms from 378 ms to 55 ms. The atlas also documents data-quality issues, several of which correct the dataset's own documentation. It is published as a website and a single machine-readable file, with open-source code and a scheme of time-aware labels. Everything is open under CC BY 4.0 and MIT licences. The engine, schema and timing tools carry over unchanged, and the aim is to describe many other datasets the same way.

♻ ☆ Skew-Induced Insertion Loss Deviation (SILD) and FOM_SILD: Metrics for Quantifying P/N Skew Effects in High-Speed Channels
David Nozadze, Zurab Kiguradze, Amendra Koul, Mike Sapozhnikov
The rise of AI workloads and growing data center demands have driven the need for ultra-high-speed interconnects exceeding 200 Gb/s. As unit intervals (UI) shrink, even a few picoseconds of P/N skew can degrade serializer-deserializer (SerDes) performance. Traditional methods for quantifying skew fall short in capturing its impact. We introduce two new metrics: 1) Skew-Induced Insertion Loss Deviation (SILD) and 2) its complementary Figure of Merit (FOM_SILD), analytically developed to assess P/N skew effects. Measured S-parameters confirm FOM_SILD reciprocity, while simulations of 224G PAM4 SerDes show strong correlation with bit error rate (BER) trends. This approach offers a robust framework for analyzing skew in next-generation ultra-high-speed interconnects.
♻ ☆ Practical Approaches to Quantifying Intra-Pair Skew Impact via Insertion Loss Deviation
David Nozadze, Zurab Kiguradze, Amendra Koul, Sayed Ashraf Mamun, Mike Sapozhnikov
The surge in AI workloads and escalating data center requirements have created demand for ultra-high-speed interconnects exceeding 200 Gb/s. As unit intervals (UI) shrink, even a few picoseconds of intra-pair skew can significantly degrade serializer-deserializer (SerDes) performance. To quantify the impact of intra-pair skew, conventional time-domain methods are often unreliable for coupled interconnects due to skew variations across voltage levels, while frequency-domain approaches frequently fail to address reciprocity and symmetry issues. This can result in channels that meet skew specifications in one direction but not the other, despite the inherently reciprocal nature of skew impact. To address these limitations, we introduce two new reciprocal parameters for quantifying intra-pair skew effects: Skew-Induced Insertion Loss Deviation (SILD) and its complementary Figure of Merit (FOM SILD). Measurements conducted using 224 Gb/s SerDes IP and a variety of channels with different intra-pair skews demonstrate a strong correlation between FOM SILD and bit error rate (BER). Results show that when FOM SILD is below 0.2-0.3 dB, BER remains stable, indicating minimal signal integrity degradation; however, BER increases noticeably as FOM SILD exceeds 0.3 dB. Statistical analysis across more than 3,000 high-speed twinax cables reveals that the majority exhibit FOM SILD values less than 0.1 dB, underscoring the practical relevance of the proposed metrics for high-speed interconnect assessment.

Mattia Piana, Giovanni Angelo Alghisi, Anna Valeria Guglielmi, Giovanni Perin, Francesco Gringoli, Stefano Tomasin
We introduce the broadband reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) channel (BRISC) dataset. The dataset comprises measurements of channel state information (CSI) collected at 5.530 GHz using a 256-element RIS with binary states. In the measurement campaign, the transmitter and receiver are two software-defined radios (SDRs), phase-synchronized via an OctoClock, where the transmitter (receiver) is equipped with one (two) antenna(s). To manage complexity, the RIS elements are grouped into blocks of different sizes, where all elements within a block share the same state. CSIs have been captured for multiple a) transmitter positions (and fixed receiver location), b) RIS element-grouping granularity, and c) RIS configurations. Furthermore, we calibrated the parameters of state-of-the-art RIS channel models to fit the measured CSI. With approximately 10 000 configurations explored per transmitting position, BRISC serves as a robust benchmark in communication applications.

Haotian Zhai, Bernd-Peter Paris
Recursive (IIR) filters realized as cascaded second-order sections (biquads) offer both design generality and robustness against coefficient quantization. However, their inherent sample-to-sample feedback dependency poses a fundamental obstacle to parallel computation. This paper reformulates the biquad difference equation as a banded block-Toeplitz linear system. It relies on a stride-$N$ permutation that maps a group of $NL$ samples into a block-tridiagonal structure whose entries are scalar multiples of identity and shift matrices. Within this framework, two data-parallel algorithms are developed which, to the best of our knowledge, are the fastest, single-core IIR filter implementations reported to date. A partial LU (PH) factorization preserves the sparse block structure and a cyclic reduction reduces the sequential dependency depth from $\mathcal{O}(N)$ to $\mathcal{O}(\log_2 N)$. For a cascade of $K$ biquads, the intermediate permutations between successive sections cancel exactly, so that only a single pair of permutations is required for the entire cascade. Exact block-level operation counts are derived for every algorithmic stage and validated against cycle-accurate measurements on three micro-architectures supporting AVX2 SIMD instructions. Experimental results for a 16th-order system show that the proposed multi-block algorithms reduce clock cycles per sample by up to $10\times$ compared to scalar filtering, with both algorithms scaling favorably on newer architectures. On a single Meteor Lake core, cyclic reduction achieves approximately 616 MS/s---four times the throughput of Intel's vendor-tuned IPP library.

Giovanni Di Gennaro, Amedeo Buonanno, Gianmarco Romano, Francesco Verde, Stefano Buzzi, Francesco A. N. Palmieri
In cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output systems, downlink power control is essential to ensure uniformly high service quality across users. Existing solutions range from computationally demanding centralized optimization to scalable distributed schemes with limited fairness. This letter proposes an unsupervised, physics-informed framework that directly optimizes max-min fairness without optimal labels or user position information. The method scales with the number of UEs, requires no retraining when the number of UEs changes, and admits a fully scalable extension. Numerical results show that it nearly doubles the worst-user spectral efficiency over existing scalable schemes.

♻ ☆ Foundation Models for Wireless Communications: From PHY Intelligence to Network Autonomy
Le Liang, Jiajia Guo, Jun Zhang, Chan-Byoung Chae, Lu Lu, Shugong Xu, Octavia A. Dobre, Shi Jin, Geoffrey Ye Li
6G networks will introduce unprecedented complexity, which calls for a paradigm shift in network optimization and management. Artificial intelligence (AI)-based solutions, especially those enabled by the recently developed foundation models, have been recognized as promising candidates. Foundation models are large-scale AI models with general-purpose feature extraction capabilities, and once trained on massive amounts of data, they can be adapted to solve a wide range of downstream tasks, either in a zero-shot manner or with few-shot fine-tuning. This article provides a comprehensive overview of how foundation models are reshaping physical-layer processing and wireless resource management across three progressive paradigms. First, we examine the adaptation of off-the-shelf pre-trained foundation models to various wireless tasks. Second, we explore wireless-native foundation models, built from scratch on wireless data to bridge cross-domain modality gaps and capture universal wireless-domain physical characteristics. Third, we highlight agentic foundation models, which elevate static data processing into autonomous, reasoning-driven network orchestration. Furthermore, we discuss the impact of applying foundation models to emerging 6G frontiers, including integrated sensing and communications (ISAC), new multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) architectures, semantic communications, and system-level network autonomy. Finally, we identify critical open challenges and opportunities, charting a promising path toward fully intelligent and adaptive wireless networks.

Yunxin Geng, Shaopeng Feng, Xuekun Hao, Zijian Guo, Shengfeng Wang, Rui Ding, Kan Zheng, Zhiqing Wei, Weiwei Jiang, Zhiyong Feng
The sixth-generation (6G) landscape demands a profound architectural evolution toward a unified, collaborative ecosystem that integrates satellite and terrestrial segments to provide ubiquitous global connectivity. Nevertheless, conventional independent management paradigms are increasingly challenged by the profound spatiotemporal nonstationarity of low-Earth orbit (LEO) channels and the volatile demands of massive heterogeneous services. To address these challenges, this study focuses on the architectural design of space-ground integrated networks (SGINs) and investigates elastic deployment strategies tailored to heterogeneous 6G service requirements. We first review the development trends in SGIN and then summarize typical application scenarios into two categories, along with their associated challenges and constraints. After that, a hierarchical space-ground collaborative network (SGCN) architecture is proposed to support achieving larger network capability, extensive continuous coverage, and enhanced spectral efficiency, which is evaluated through three representative scenarios with progressive baselines. Subsequently, a service-aware deployment strategy is introduced to further establish the engineering feasibility of the proposed architecture.

♻ ☆ ACHEM: A Real-Time Digital Twin Framework with Channel and Radio Emulation
Anil Gurses, Mihail L. Sichitiu
Digital twins are becoming an important tool for designing, developing, testing, and optimizing next-generation wireless communication systems. Over the past decade, system softwarization has become a reality, and wireless communication systems are no exception. Software-Defined Radios (SDRs), in general, and Universal Software Radio Peripherals (USRPs), in particular, are often used for prototyping and testing advanced wireless systems. Unfortunately, there is currently no end-to-end, software-based, general-purpose testing environment for SDR-based systems: developers often rely on benchtop setups or even small testbeds, but those are costly and cumbersome to build. At the other end of the spectrum, simulations often rely on simplified channel/radio models and typically do not execute full-stack production code, which can increase development effort and reduce fidelity. In this paper, we propose ACHEM (A Channel Emulator), the first software-based, end-to-end wireless channel emulation environment and toolset for communication systems based on SDRs, specifically USRPs. With the proposed emulator and toolkit, any USRP-based system can be fully emulated at the I/Q level in a pure digital environment without requiring specialized hardware (e.g., vehicles, USRPs, FPGAs, or GPUs). The proposed emulator supports multiple transmitters and receivers, MIMO communications, multiple frequencies, heterogeneous sampling rates, real-time node mobility through vehicle emulation, antenna radiation patterns, and various channel models. ACHEM facilitates wireless digital twin development and deployment. ACHEM is validated with several popular open-source USRP-based wireless communication applications, including GNU Radio, srsRAN 4G/5G, and OpenAirInterface.

Hangsong Yan, Hong Yang, Shu Sun
This paper establishes a comprehensive theoretical framework for the continuous-to-discrete modeling of spatially stationary holographic MIMO (HMIMO) channels utilizing the Nystrom method with Gauss-Legendre quadrature (NGLQ). Starting with an operator-theoretic analysis of the NGLQ method, we prove that its quadrature error exhibits a super-exponential decay. Furthermore, we derive a spatial sampling threshold, termed computational degrees of freedom (cDoF), which reveals a π/2 oversampling penalty over the physical DoF for 1D arrays, compounding to a 68% computational redundancy for 2D separable grids. To address the ill-conditioning of the eigenvalue decomposition (EVD) problem inherent to the Nystrom discretization, we invoke the multidimensional Szego-Widom asymptotic expansion. The principal barriers to engineering deployment include limited and biased datasets, weak out-of-distribution generalization, insufficient physical consistency, unsafe online adaptation, embedded-resource constraints, and the absence of standardized benchmarks. Future research should prioritize uncertainty-aware and physics-informed learning, safe simulation-to-reality transfer, lightweight edge deployment, distributed coordination, reproducible evaluation, and digital-twin-assisted development.

Under some mild regularity conditions, we show that Bellman-side NDE can be characterized by a heat equation. This characterization identifies the class of Bellman-side NDE functions, and further yields a decomposition of a generic cost-to-go function into a Bellman-side NDE component and a dual-effect component.

Learning safe policies that generalize to unseen environments is difficult under bounded actuation, where an unsafe decision may become unrecoverable. Conventional control barrier function (CBF) filters enforce only instantaneous safety and ignore future recoverability. We propose SAFTER (Safety-Aware Filtering Through Explicit Recoverability), which embeds a differentiable, closed-form backup-CBF filter into Soft Actor-Critic training. SAFTER unifies current safety, finite-horizon backup safety, terminal recoverability, and input admissibility into a single differentiable certificate. Its CBF condition yields an exact minimum-intervention projection without iterative online optimization. In quadruped navigation, SAFTER reaches 90% training success with 30.6% fewer transitions than Vanilla SAC and 34.1-35.1% fewer than current-state CBF-filtered SAC baselines. Across unseen simulated environments, SAFTER improves success by up to 42.4 and 61.4 percentage points over the state-of-the-art methods CBF-RL and SEA-Nav, respectively, and achieves 73.3% and 76.7% success on two real-world navigation maps. Ablations identify accurate differentiation through the safety filter as a key contributor to robustness, in which replacing the projection Jacobian with the identity approximation reduces success rate in a High-Shift environment from 61.4% to 6.2%. These results show that recoverability-aware filtering serves as both a runtime safety mechanism and a learning mechanism for sample-efficient, robust policies.
comment: 24 pages, 6 figures
♻ ☆ Skew-Induced Insertion Loss Deviation (SILD) and FOM_SILD: Metrics for Quantifying P/N Skew Effects in High-Speed Channels
David Nozadze, Zurab Kiguradze, Amendra Koul, Mike Sapozhnikov
The rise of AI workloads and growing data center demands have driven the need for ultra-high-speed interconnects exceeding 200 Gb/s. As unit intervals (UI) shrink, even a few picoseconds of P/N skew can degrade serializer-deserializer (SerDes) performance. Traditional methods for quantifying skew fall short in capturing its impact. We introduce two new metrics: 1) Skew-Induced Insertion Loss Deviation (SILD) and 2) its complementary Figure of Merit (FOM_SILD), analytically developed to assess P/N skew effects. Measured S-parameters confirm FOM_SILD reciprocity, while simulations of 224G PAM4 SerDes show strong correlation with bit error rate (BER) trends. This approach offers a robust framework for analyzing skew in next-generation ultra-high-speed interconnects.
♻ ☆ Principles of Robot Autonomy
Daniele Gammelli, Joseph Lorenzetti, Katie Luo, Gioele Zardini, Marco Pavone
Autonomous robots are moving rapidly from research labs into everyday life - on roads, in the air, in warehouses, and in space. Robot autonomy is no longer solely an academic pursuit, but a collection of mature, field-tested methods and tools that practitioners rely on in real-world deployments. This book offers a clear, unified introduction to the methods that make this possible. Built on decades of teaching at Stanford, the text develops the core elements of modern autonomy stacks within a single conceptual framework, bridging classical robotics and modern physical AI. Every major topic is paired with hands-on Jupyter notebooks and implementation-driven exercises, so readers build practical intuition alongside theoretical understanding. The result is a principled, accessible, and deployment-aware foundation for anyone seeking to design, analyze, or contribute to the next generation of autonomous systems. This is a comprehensive resource for students, engineers, and researchers entering one of today's fastest-growing fields.
comment: 531 pages. Pre-publication version of a book forthcoming from Cambridge University Press, posted with the permission of the publisher
♻ ☆ On the Gradient Domination of the LQG Problem
Kasra Fallah, Leonardo F. Toso, James Anderson
We consider solutions to the linear quadratic Gaussian (LQG) regulator problem via policy gradient (PG) methods. Although PG methods have demonstrated strong theoretical guarantees in solving the linear quadratic regulator (LQR) problem, despite its nonconvex landscape, their theoretical understanding in the LQG setting remains limited. Notably, the LQG problem lacks gradient dominance in the classical parameterization, i.e., with a dynamic controller, which hinders global convergence guarantees. In this work, we study a PG method for the LQG problem by adopting an alternative parameterization of the set of stabilizing controllers and employing a lifting argument. We refer to this parameterization as a history representation of the control input as it is parameterized by past input and output data from the previous p time-steps. Under this parameterization, the infinite-history LQG optimization reduces to an equivalent static state-feedback LQR problem, allowing us to recover gradient dominance and smoothness. For finite history length p, we establish model-based and model-free convergence guarantees up to a geometrically decaying history-truncation error.
comment: Refined theoretical results and improved analysis in the revised version
♻ ☆ Bayesian Ambiguity Contraction-based Adaptive Robust Markov Decision Processes for Adversarial Surveillance Missions
Jimin Choi, Max Z. Li
Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCAs) are envisioned to enable autonomous Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance (ISR) missions in contested environments, where adversaries may act strategically to deceive or evade detection. These missions pose challenges due to model uncertainty and the need for safe, real-time decision-making. Robust Markov Decision Processes (RMDPs) provide worst-case guarantees but are limited by static ambiguity sets that capture initial uncertainty without adapting to new observations. This paper presents an adaptive RMDP framework tailored to ISR missions with CCAs. We introduce a mission-specific formulation in which the CCA alternates between movement and sensing states. Adversarial uncertainty is represented by finite threat prototypes defining observation, exposure, and state-action transition models. Our approach incrementally refines policies by eliminating inconsistent threat models, allowing the CCA to move from worst-case protection toward more efficient mission policies while maintaining robustness. We establish fixed point stability, agreement with nominal planning as credible sets identify the true node-specific threat prototypes, and a conservative expected value guarantee while those prototypes remain credible. Experiments under Gaussian and non-Gaussian threat models across diverse network topologies show higher mission rewards and fewer exposure events compared to nominal and static robust planners.
♻ ☆ Real-Time Disturbance-Aware Koopman Model Predictive Control for Quadrotors in Spatially Varying Winds
Stella Kombo, Masih Haseli, Alejandro A. Stefan-Zavala, Peter I. Renn, Morteza Gharib, Joel W. Burdick
Reliable quadrotor flight in disturbed environments requires predictive models that remain accurate as unmodeled aerodynamic effects change during deployment. We introduce a disturbance-aware Koopman Control Family (DA-KCF) framework that preserves an offline-identified nominal model while learning only a disturbance-induced correction online. A reference-dependent KCF is first learned from simulation data and calibrated using limited hardware data. During deployment, the nominal KCF remains fixed while a lightweight residual ensemble learns a low-dimensional disturbance correction from causal state-command-state transitions. The Adaptive DA-KCF model is incorporated into MPC, where disturbance corrections are evaluated along the prediction horizon to optimize position and yaw references sent to the onboard stabilizing controller. Hardware experiments on a nano-quadrotor under uniform wind and a spatially varying wake demonstrate that online adaptation improves multi-step prediction and trajectory tracking as disturbance-induced model mismatch increases, while satisfying real-time control requirements.
♻ ☆ Region of Attraction Estimation for Linear Quadratic Regulator, Linear and Robust Model Predictive Control on a Two-Wheeled Inverted Pendulum
Lorenzo Fici, Dalim Wahby, Alvaro Detailleur, Matthieu Barreau, Guillaume Ducard
Nonlinear underactuated systems such as two-wheeled inverted pendulums (TWIPs) exhibit a limited region of attraction (RoA), which defines the set of initial conditions from which the closed-loop system converges to the equilibrium. The RoA of nonlinear and constrained systems is generally nonconvex and analytically intractable, requiring numerical or approximate estimation methods. This work investigates the estimation of the RoA for a TWIP stabilized under three model-based control strategies: saturated linear quadratic regulator (LQR), linear model predictive control (MPC), and constraint tightening MPC (CTMPC). We first derive a Lyapunov-based invariant set that provides a certified inner approximation of the RoA. Since this analytical bound is highly conservative, a Monte Carlo-based estimation procedure is then employed to obtain a more representative approximation of the RoA, capturing how the controllers behave beyond the analytically guaranteed region. The proposed methodology combines analytical guarantees with data-driven estimation, providing both a formally certified inner bound and an empirical characterization of the RoA, offering a practical way to evaluate controller performance without relying solely on conservative analytical bounds or purely empirical simulation.
♻ ☆ Proposals and challenges for zero-knowledge verification of frontier AI training
Pierre Peigné, Ky Nguyen, Paul Wang
Proposals for Frontier AI rules often use cumulative training compute as the main criterion for identifying high-impact models. Recent governance analyses call zero-knowledge proofs promising but currently impractical at frontier scale [26, 4]. We argue this barrier reflects the current paradigm, not a fundamental limit. Our frontier dense-pre-training design combines a pre-committed specification, inter-node network observations, and live Merkle commitments to intermediate computation. Our reference zero-knowledge virtual machine (zkVM) provides a succinct proof layer with native BF16/FP32 precompiles. We qualitatively compare zkVMs, custom circuits, and direct interactive audits by transferability, soundness, and cost. Public randomness beacons are a separate audit-selection choice. At challenged positions, proofs check the committed computation against declared BF16/FP32 semantics bit-for-bit. A private training specification targets model-architecture confidentiality. Genesis proofs cover initialisation; then, in-training step proofs verify selected steps across the run. Ex-ante attestations enforce policy-relevant claims as running invariants on every proved step. Together they create a governance-auditable training record. Detection-probability formulas quantify sampling guarantees from the sampling budget and the share of computation altered. We give numerical examples and explain what sampling does not cover. We note, however, that weight smuggling could reuse or merge weights trained elsewhere without charging that work to the current run. We then argue that regimes with global training budgets are more robust than regimes with per-run FLOP caps. This advantage depends on counting all contributing training. We catalogue remaining research and engineering problems for external contributors.

♻ ☆ Physics-Informed Koopman Learning for Data-Efficient System Identification of Automated Vehicle Dynamics
Hangyu Li, Yiming Meng, Zhaohui Liang, Yunqing Xiao, Yuxuan Chen, Bofeng Cao, Shixiao Liang, Jiaxi Liu, Haotian Shi, Xiaopeng Li
Understanding how a particular automated vehicle reacts to nearby traffic can improve motion prediction, control development, traffic simulation, and safety evaluation. However, commercial automated driving systems are proprietary, and single encounters may provide only a few seconds of noisy data. Standard physical models are interpretable but inflexible, whereas neural models are often data-hungry. We propose a physics-informed Koopman framework that combines a calibrated car-following law with a correction learned from the observations. A weak-form estimator learns this correction from velocity measurements integrated over time, avoiding noise-sensitive numerical differentiation. The resulting continuous-time model predicts the follower's response and provides interpretable measures of driving behavior. Experiments on OpenACC and CATS-CF evaluate 5-, 7-, and 11-second histories. Averaged over these histories, the constant-time-headway branch reduces speed prediction error by 16.0% and 15.4% on OpenACC and CATS-CF, respectively, relative to the best neural baselines. The PI-Koopman branches achieve the lowest mean speed and gap errors among the physical and neural comparators. Weak-form estimation reduces acceleration-field reconstruction error by 74.5% in noisy known-law simulations and noise-induced field perturbation by 91.6% in paired real-vehicle measurements. The same PI-Koopman system identification supports following-mode recognition with an approximately eleven-fold difference in median residual variance between human drivers and automated vehicles, and a single residual threshold achieves 85.4% balanced accuracy. The branch informed by the intelligent driver model takes a median 17 to 26 ms for identification and forecasting on the tested central processing units, supporting frequent target adaptation.
comment: 13 pages, 9 figures. The CATS-CF dataset and code are available at https://github.com/CATS-Lab/PI-Koopman
♻ ☆ Initialization-Free LEO Doppler Positioning via Semidefinite Relaxation: A Cold-Start Approach
Baoshan Song, Weisong Wen, Qi Zhang, Bing Xu, Penggao Yan, Yuan Li, Li-Ta Hsu
Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite Doppler measurements offer an alternative source of positioning information for Internet of Things devices when Global Navigation Satellite System signals are unavailable. Conventional local optimisation methods depend on an accurate initial position and can fail during a complete cold start. We propose an initialization-free LEO Doppler positioning framework based on semidefinite relaxation. The method reformulates the nonlinear positioning problem into a semidefinite programme to obtain a receiver position estimate without prior location knowledge. We analyse relaxation tightness under noiseless conditions and derive sufficient noise bounds under parameter disturbances. Simulations and field experiments using opportunistic Iridium-NEXT signals evaluate initialization sensitivity, positioning accuracy and computational cost. In the field experiment, the proposed method achieves a three-dimensional positioning error of 140 m without an initial position, whereas local solvers converge to poor solutions under large initial offsets. Using the semidefinite estimate to initialise Gauss-Newton or Dog-Leg reduces the positioning error to 130 m. The framework provides a cold-start initialization stage for subsequent local refinement in opportunistic LEO positioning. The implementation and datasets are publicly available to support reproducibility and further research.
comment: Revised version
♻ ☆ Latency-Neutral Passive Cyber Monitoring for Grid-Edge Operational Technology Networks
Damian Byrne, Emad Abukhousa, Jason Reed, Saman Zonouz
Deterministic industrial networks often present an operational trade-off between maintaining microsecond timing of primary control loops and capturing security telemetry. This work investigates the engineering feasibility of the Operational Technology Supervisor (OTSV), a three-tier passive monitoring framework designed to resolve this visibility challenge within timing-sensitive grid-edge infrastructure. By utilizing a Layer-3-unconfigured passive ingestion mode on bare-metal hardware via a physical switched port analyzer (SPAN) loop, the deep packet inspection engine is isolated from the production network, implementing a software-enforced unidirectional export policy. Performance validation conducted over a continuous audit comprising 32,927 active-monitoring round-trip time (RTT) samples yielded stable latency distributions across a laboratory power-monitoring loop running Modbus TCP and IEC 61850 MMS protocols. The measured latency delta between the unmonitored baseline and the active monitoring state was less than 0.12 milliseconds, supporting the feasibility of continuous high-fidelity security observation alongside stringent grid-edge metering timing bounds without measurably degrading the monitored reporting path.
comment: 5 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Accepted for presentation at the IEEE PES Grid Edge Technologies Conference and Exposition 2027
♻ ☆ The Cheap Hours Don't Stay Cheap: Price-Chasing Data Centers Reshape Grids and Markets
Shijie Pan, Zaint A. Alexakis, Charalambos Konstantinou
Data centers unsettle the paradigm of location-bound electricity demand: computing workloads can migrate across sites and hours, whereas facilities and grid connections remain fixed. This mobility reduces electricity costs but reshapes the spatiotemporal structure of nodal prices. A model-driven framework couples US wholesale market signals with optimal fleet scheduling, showing how their interaction alters prices and other participants' responses. Greater flexibility enlarges savings yet can erode network benefits: in a Texas study, temporal shifting and cross-site allocation each relieve congestion, but their combination leaves total congestion nearly unchanged. At continental scale, computing demand gravitating toward cheaper electricity narrows price differences and compresses the low-price hours storage arbitrage relies on, threatening storage investment recovery. Cost-minimizing scheduling may therefore undermine grid-supporting resources. Comparing job-level and aggregate fleet representations reveals a trade-off between operational visibility and information disclosure, informing requirements and incentives that could turn workload mobility into a lever for system-wide efficiency.
♻ ☆ TNODEV: Toolbox for Neural ODE Verification
Abdelrahman Sayed Sayed, Pierre-Jean Meyer, Mohamed Ghazel
Neural ordinary differential equations (neural ODE) gained attention in safety critical settings such as continuous-time controllers for cyber-physical systems and classifiers integrated into automated decision pipelines, raising the question whether their behavior can be formally verified. Existing tools dedicated to neural ODE provide only a single reachability call without iterative input-set refinement, limiting the precision of their verdicts to whatever one reachability call can deliver. We present TNODEV, the first formal verifier for neural ODE that integrates a falsification checker, a fast interval-based reachability backend based on continuous-time mixed monotonicity, a verification and refinement loop with three input-set splitting heuristics, and a parallel scheduler in a single end-to-end pipeline. TNODEV supports safe-set inclusion verification on pure neural ODE, neural ODE in closed loop with a neural network controller and general neural ODE (GNODE), with the safe set specified either as an interval or as the half-space intersection induced by a target classification label. We evaluate TNODEV on a range of benchmarks across safe-set inclusion and classification-robustness properties, including a direct reachability comparison against NNV 2.0 and CORA and a verification comparison against NNV 2.0 on MNIST general neural ODE classifiers.
comment: 44 pages, 10 figures, Accepted in TMLR 2026. Code available at https://github.com/ab-sayed/TNODEV
♻ ☆ A Novel Schur Decomposition-Based Weight Projection Method for Stable State-Space Neural-Network Architectures
Sergio Vanegas, Lasse Lensu, Fredy Ruiz
Building black-box models for dynamical systems from data is a challenging problem in machine learning, especially when asymptotic stability guarantees are required. In this paper, we introduce a novel stability-ensuring and backpropagation-compatible projection scheme based on the Schur decomposition for the state matrix of linear discrete-time state-space layers, as well as an alternative pre-factorized formulation of the methodology. The proposed methods dynamically project the quasi-triangular factor of the state matrix's real Schur decomposition onto its nearest stable peer, ensuring stable dynamics with minimal overparameterization. Experiments on synthetic linear systems demonstrate that, despite a marginal increase in computational complexity, the method achieves accuracy and convergence rates comparable to those of state-of-the-art stable-system identification techniques. Furthermore, the lower weight count facilitates convergence during training without sacrificing accuracy in stacked neural-network architectures with static nonlinearities targeting real-world datasets. These results suggest that the Schur-based projection provides a numerically robust framework for identifying complex dynamics on par with the state of the art while satisfying strict asymptotic-stability requirements.
comment: 32 pages, 13 figures. Source code at https://codeberg.org/sergiovaneg/SchurSS
♻ ☆ Learning Altruistic Collaboration in Heterogeneous Multi-Team Systems
Riwa Karam, Ruoyu Lin, Brooks A. Butler, Magnus Egerstedt
This paper studies heterogeneous multi-team collaboration through dynamic robot allocation, where the robots themselves are treated as transferable resources. Leveraging Hamilton's rule from ecology as an altruistic decision-making mechanism, we propose a multi-team collaborative resource allocation framework with heterogeneous capabilities, transfer costs, and capability-dependent contributions. The resulting general heterogeneous resource assignment problem is combinatorial and is shown to be NP-hard. To address scalability, we develop a graph neural network policy under centralized training and decentralized execution that approximates the altruistic allocations based on Hamilton's rule. The model operates over the team interaction graph and predicts robot-level transfer decisions and subsequent robot-to-team assignments. The proposed approach is evaluated in a fire-fighting scenario against exact optimization and multi-step simulations, quantifying allocation quality, decision computation, and fire suppression. Five paired physical testbed trials with 15 robots compare learned reallocation with fixed team membership; the GNN reaches the modeled fire stopping threshold in all five trials, compared with two for static allocation.
♻ ☆ Optimal Control of Behavioral-Feedback SIR Epidemic Model
Martina Alutto, Leonardo Cianfanelli, Giacomo Como, Fabio Fagnani, Francesca Parise
We consider a behavioral-feedback SIR epidemic model, in which the infection rate depends in feedback on the fractions of susceptible and infected agents. Contrary to the classic SIR dynamics, the considered model allows one to account for endogenous adaptation mechanisms of the agents in response to the epidemics, such as voluntary social distancing, or the adoption of face masks. For this model, we formulate an optimal control problem for a social planner that has the ability to reduce the infection rate to keep the infection curve below a certain threshold within an infinite time horizon, while minimizing the intervention cost. Based on the dynamic properties of the model, we prove that, under quite general conditions on the infection rate, the filling-the-box strategy is the optimal control. This strategy consists in letting the epidemics spread without intervention until the threshold is reached, then applying the minimum control that leaves the fraction of infected individuals constantly at the threshold until the reproduction number becomes less than one and the infection naturally fades out. Our contribution enhances the understanding of epidemic management while accounting for adaptive human behavior, offering novel insights for robust containment strategies.

♻ ☆ Traffic State Prediction and Control Using a Koopman Operator Framework with Polynomial Observables
Shakib Mustavee, Arvind Singh, Shaurya Agarwal
In this paper, we develop a Koopman operator framework for modeling and control of traffic flow governed by the Lighthill--Whitham--Richards (LWR) conservation law. We show that the nonlinear dynamics induced by the Greenshields flow--density relation naturally motivate a dictionary of polynomial observables, while the controlled dynamics become bilinear in the lifted Koopman coordinates. A reduced-order Koopman model is identified from spatio-temporal traffic-density snapshots and used as the prediction model in a model predictive control (MPC) framework for ramp metering. The resulting Koopman-MPC is compared with two predictive control baselines that use, respectively, a fixed linearized LWR model and the nonlinear finite-volume LWR model. In a one-hour freeway experiment, the Koopman-based controller maintains the traffic density below the critical Greenshields value and closely reproduces the behavior of the nonlinear PDE-based MPC, with a maximum-density difference below 1%. The Koopman predictor also reduces the mean online model-evaluation cost by approximately one order of magnitude relative to the nonlinear PDE predictor. In contrast, the linearized LWR predictor is computationally cheaper but exhibits substantially larger prediction errors and yields a more conservative metering policy. These results demonstrate that the analytical structure of the nonlinear traffic conservation law can be exploited to construct an interpretable data-driven surrogate for efficient traffic prediction and control
Logic in Computer Science
☆ TrustedCode: Evaluating Large Language Models for Developing Trusted Code through Automated Program Verification
Muhammad Danial, Muhammad Taimoor Khan
Recent reports, such as "Who is using AI to code?", indicate that approximately 30\% of Python code contributions to GitHub are AI-generated. Given the inherent unreliability of this code, formal verification emerges as a promising approach to establish trust in software correctness. Although leveraging large language models (LLMs) for formal verification has garnered increasing attention, practical adoption remains limited due to the challenges in writing formal specifications and verifying program correctness against them. Existing tools predominantly support verification for languages such as Java and C, with minimal support for Python. We present TrustedCode, an automated framework for verifying AI-generated Python code. TrustedCode uses LLMs to (i) type-check Python code, (ii) translate it into WhyML via the Why3 framework, and (iii) verify it against formal specifications using Why3 back-end automated theorem provers. Our method integrates chain-of-thought prompting through LangGraph to identify and address LLM limitations in specification generation and proving the specified programs. To evaluate TrustedCode, we conducted experiments on ten Python programs of varying complexity. Our analysis reveals that 50\% of the observed errors stem from domain knowledge gaps, 30\% from syntactic inaccuracies, and the remaining 20\% from semantic and type-related issues. These findings underscore the importance of targeted improvements in LLM-guided formal verification workflows for Python. TrustedCode is an open source tool available at: \href{github.com/mtaimoorkhan/TrustedCode}{github.com/mtaimoorkhan/TrustedCode}. The video demonstration is available at: \href{youtu.be/Nr5I2g8ec-s}{youtu.be/Nr5I2g8ec-s}
☆ Coherent differentiation with a monoid of degrees: derivatives, Taylor expansion, finite differences...
Thomas Ehrhard, Aymeric Walch
Coherent differentiation has been introduced a few years ago as a refinement of the (categorical semantics of the) differential lambda-calculus and of differential linear logic, compatible with the determinism of computation, and hence in categories where addition of morphisms in the hom-sets is only partially defined. In this setting differentiation is implemented by a kind of ''tangent functor'', with the difference that it maps an object to its object of summable tuples rather to a tangent bundle. In our earlier work, these tuples were pairs in the case of simple differentiation, and families indexed by integers when dealing with Taylor expansion and the Fa{à} di Bruno formula. We push this idea further, considering now tuples indexed by an arbitrary commutative partial monoid satisfying a nonnegativity condition. The monoid structure on these indices plays a crucial role in the definition of the ''differential'' calculus associated with this ''tangent functor''. In that way, and without changing the general categorical infrastructure of coherent differentiation, this theory accommodates new notions of ''differentiation'' of which we describe several instances. Among many others, such notions include various forms of finite differences as well as Taylor expansion truncated at any fixed degree, and finite Taylor expansion of a fixed finite degree with a remainder.
☆ Two Sides of the Same Proof: Extraction and Projection in Choreographic Programming
Matteo Acclavio, Giulia Manara, Fabrizio Montesi, Marco Peressotti
A new approach to the theory of choreographic languages has recently been proposed, based on the interpretation of choreographies with finite behaviors as proofs in an extension of linear logic. This paper further develops this approach to cyclic proofs to be capable of representing infinite behaviors, and prove a completeness result for choreographies with respect to the class of lock-free networks. We show that in a choreographies-as-proofs correspondence, the proof equivalence induced by rule permutations corresponds to bisimilarity, and that, under adequate assumption on the procedure definitions, the proof search procedure has a finite search space, and can be used to extract a choreography from a network.
☆ Any colour you like, as long as it's UIP: Semi-simplicial types from weakenings and thinnings
Thorsten Altenkirch
We explain an attempt to define semi-simplicial types (SST) in homotopy type theory by first defining a small type theory whose contexts are exactly the data of semi-simplicial types, constructing $\mathrm{SST}\,n$ uniformly in that syntax, and then interpreting the syntax in the universe. The syntax can be defined without any truncation and without K, and the construction of $\mathrm{SST}\,n$ goes through. The naive interpretation does not: it transports along the semantic images of equations that hold only propositionally, and making these transports agree needs uniqueness of identity proofs (UIP) for the semantic types. Moving the problem into the syntax, by making composition a constructor of a higher inductive-inductive type (HIIT), does not remove it either: it reappears as a coherence problem in the syntax. Fording the HIIT (storing equations instead of computed indices), with conditional rules, makes the syntax provably a set. This is UIP for the syntax, obtained by encode-decode, and it does not by itself restrict the semantics; but the naive interpretation of the conditional rules again needs UIP for the semantic types. A semantics into groupoids that avoids UIP will be discussed in a separate note. The Agda development accompanying this note is in the repository https://github.com/txa/sst-new.
☆ Deciding Scale Placement in MXFP4 Dot Products with Integer Arithmetic
Shreyas Vinayakumar
The Open Compute Project's microscaling (MX) family includes MXFP4, which stores 32 four-bit elements with a shared power-of-two scale. When lowering a dot-product reduction, a compiler can apply these scales before the reduction, or defer scaling until afterwards. Although equivalent over real numbers, these formulations can produce different IEEE binary32 results through overflow or underflow, with equivalence also depending on the reduction tree. We study the legality of compiler rewrites in either direction by deriving conditions under which the two formulations are bitwise equivalent. To decide rewrite legality, we construct an integer state machine that exploits the finite element alphabet and shared power-of-two scales, modeling overflow, NaN, and subnormal rounding. We prove its faithfulness under bounded scale codes and integer coefficients, yielding an exact encoding of the equivalence query in quantifier-free linear integer arithmetic (QF_LIA). For MXFP4, we derive a closed-form sufficient upper bound on the sum of scale exponents for any fixed binary reduction tree within the supported coefficient range. This bound depends on the size of the largest proper subtree. For four tree shapes at block lengths $k\in\{2,3,4,8,16,32\}$ and two shapes at $k=64$, SMT finds counterexamples when this upper bound is increased by one exponent step. Against the standard direct encoding in quantifier-free floating-point arithmetic (QF_FP), on matched queries cvc5 proves the integer version in seconds but reaches a configured one-CPU-hour limit on the floating-point proof even at $k=2$. The implementation was cross-checked using an independent floating-point encoding, exhaustive and stratified binary32 execution, and GPU replay of counterexamples. An MLIR lowering prototype demonstrates selection between the two formulations using the certified conditions as static or runtime guards.

☆ Post-Pruning vs. Early Stopping: Which Works Better for Link Prediction with AnyBurl?
Thomas Eiter, Davide Soldà, Hai Xia
Rule-based link prediction combines symbolic and statistical artificial intelligence methods by inductively learning a set of rules from a knowledge graph (KG), with the aim of completing the graph when a query cannot be answered from the KG alone. Several systems have been proposed, and while they perform well on classical benchmarks, even compared with embedding-based systems, many of them produce a large number of rules. This compromises scalability in the query-answering phase, especially under strong hardware constraints. In this work, we investigate the behavior of AnyBurl, a state-of-the-art rule learner for link prediction, to determine whether running it for a given time and then pruning the learned rules yields better query-answering performance at test time than a simpler approach that stops rule generation earlier.
☆ VERDICT: Multi-Agent Parallel Modular Verification ICSE 2027
Tengjie Lin, Zhongyi Wang, Haokun Li, Jianwei Yin, Mingshuai Chen
Deductive verification scales to large software systems through modular reasoning, where formal contracts summarize the behavior of individual functions and enable their independent verification. Its central bottleneck is specification synthesis: constructing the contracts required for modular verification. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled automated specification synthesis at unprecedented scale. However, existing approaches remain fundamentally bottom-up, requiring callees to be verified before their callers. This dependency limits parallelism and provides no principled mechanism for resolving interprocedural inconsistencies that propagate across call chains. We present VERDICT, a multi-agent framework for parallelizing modular deductive verification of large-scale programs. VERDICT is built on two key principles. First, assumption-based parallel specification synthesis assigns an agent to each function and allows it to proceed immediately using assumed contracts for its callees, enabling verification to proceed in parallel across the program. Second, bidirectional interprocedural conflict reconciliation resolves the inconsistencies introduced by these assumptions: when a synthesized contract contradicts an assumption, agents propagate the necessary revisions both up and down the call graph until the contracts converge. Experimental results on real-world C programs show that VERDICT synthesizes higher-quality specifications than existing approaches while substantially reducing verification time. In particular, VERDICT is the first approach that scales to the complete 20,000-line X.509 parser, ruling out nearly all the potential runtime errors within hours, whereas prior tools like PREGUSS fall far short even after days of execution.
comment: Accepted at ICSE 2027
♻ ☆ Beyond LLM Judge: Mechanical Verification for Agentic Autoformalization
Anna Mei, Michael R. Douglas
We introduce a novel method for verifying Lean formalizations that goes beyond LLM-judged faithfulness. Unlike most verification methods, which rely on LLMs or trained models, our method combines LLM-based semantic review with mechanical numerical and vacuity checks, providing checkable feedback and detecting errors missed by LLM judges. We apply this method, along with our Extract-Verify-Proof autoformalization pipeline, to construct the Formalized Library of Mathematical Functions (FLMF), a partial formalization of the NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions (DLMF). On three labeled datasets, our method achieves the lowest accepted-error rate among the evaluated methods, measured as the fraction of incorrect statements accepted by the verification method. Expert review of the results also identifies translation and source defects in existing datasets. Code available at https://github.com/annamei1/FLMF-Ch7ErrFunc-Release.git.

Sirui Lu, Ruixuan Deng, Yanqiao Zhu, Zhengfeng Ji
Landmark mathematical formalizations have taken specialist teams years to complete. We present FormalFlow, a system that coordinates AI proving agents under human supervision to address statement drift and proof composition in long-horizon formalization. Drawing on software-engineering principles and practices, it uses a shared blueprint to guide nested planning, proving, and review loops. Using FormalFlow, we completed a machine-checked Lean 4 proof of the quantum soundness of the classical low individual-degree test, a core theorem underlying MIP* = RE, in 63 days. The final library contains 126,367 lines of Lean code, all generated by agents. Beyond providing a verified foundation for quantum complexity, the formalization corrects side conditions and intermediate error bounds in the published proof and improves the error exponent of the main theorem. The development record shows what it takes to trust proofs written by AI agents and provides reusable tools for verifying research mathematics at scale.
